common_name: Mary S. DeBaillon Louisiana Iris (Collected Red-Violet Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in early fall in constantly moist, humus-rich soil; this collected selection was registered by Caroline Dormon in 1942 and won the inaugural Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1948, the award later named for the collector who first recognized Louisiana irises' garden value.

directions: Mary S. DeBaillon is a red-violet (color class R3D) Louisiana iris collected from the wild and registered by Caroline Dormon in 1942, honoring Mary Swords DeBaillon, the collector whose enthusiasm helped launch organized interest in the species group. It won the first Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1948, the honor that now bears her name as the highest distinction an American Iris Society Louisiana iris can receive. Grow it in a bog bed, rain garden, or pond margin with steady moisture through spring growth, dividing crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: The Khan Louisiana Iris (Velvety Black-Violet Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fall in rich, constantly moist soil; The Khan was registered by Caroline Dormon and won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1955.

directions: The Khan carries velvety black-violet standards and falls set off by unusually brilliant orange spear signals, a dramatic combination for a mid-century Louisiana iris. Pioneering Louisiana iris breeder Caroline Dormon registered the cultivar, which went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1955. Site it in consistently damp, humus-rich soil in full sun, where its dark coloring shows best against lighter-flowered companions.

common_name: Amethyst Star Louisiana Iris (Purple Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fall in moisture-retentive soil; Amethyst Star was bred by Louisiana iris breeder Sydney DuBose and won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1960.

directions: Amethyst Star is a tall, midseason-to-late-blooming Louisiana iris in rich amethyst-purple tones, bred by Sydney DuBose. It earned the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1960, cementing DuBose's reputation among mid-century Louisiana iris hybridizers. Give it full sun and steady, abundant moisture through spring, and divide congested clumps every few years to sustain strong bloom.

common_name: Mary Dunn Louisiana Iris (Palest Orchid-Violet Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fall in rich, moist soil; Ben Hager registered Mary Dunn, naming it for the prolific California Louisiana iris hybridizer, and it won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1977.

directions: Mary Dunn bears palest orchid-violet flowers with a clear yellow signal on a compact, midseason-blooming stalk. Hybridizer Ben Hager registered it and named it in tribute to Mary Dunn, herself a highly productive Louisiana iris breeder who registered well over a hundred cultivars; the plant won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Award in 1977. Keep it in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun, and divide every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Red Velvet Elvis Louisiana Iris (Dark Red-Black Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fall in rich, constantly moist soil; Kevin Vaughn registered Red Velvet Elvis as part of his long effort to breed a true red Louisiana iris, and it won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2005.

directions: Red Velvet Elvis shows near-black dark red-black standards and falls with a lightly ruffled, velvety texture and a partly hidden orange-yellow spear signal, blooming over an unusually long early-to-late season. Kevin Vaughn registered it during his documented effort to breed a true red Louisiana iris, and the cultivar earned the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2005. Plant it in full sun with abundant, steady moisture for the richest bloom color.

common_name: Night Thunder Louisiana Iris (Dark Violet to Near-Black Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fall in rich, saturated soil; Richard Morgan registered Night Thunder, and it won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2010.

directions: Night Thunder produces ruffled, velvety flowers that shade from dark violet to near-black, with falls brightened by a bold orange steeple signal. Richard Morgan registered the cultivar, which rose to the top of Louisiana iris competition by winning the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2010. Grow it at a pond margin or in a consistently wet bed in full sun, where the dark bloom color contrasts well against the bright signal.

common_name: My Friend Dick Louisiana Iris (Currant Red Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fall in rich, moist soil; raised from a seedling by Richard Butler and introduced by M. D. Faith, My Friend Dick won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2007.

directions: My Friend Dick bears currant-red, midseason flowers with a bold golden-yellow signal. It began as a seedling raised by Richard Butler, a Little Rock lawyer and Louisiana iris enthusiast, and was introduced by M. D. Faith in Butler's honor after his death; the cultivar went on to win the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2007. Plant it in full sun with consistently wet, fertile soil for its best currant-red display.

common_name: Ginny's Choice Louisiana Iris (Blue-Violet and Gold Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fall in rich, wet soil; Wayland Rudkin registered Ginny's Choice in 2003, and it won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2012.

directions: Ginny's Choice shows ruffled, recurved blue-violet standards and falls with a yellow star steeple signal and a greenish crest, blooming midseason. Wayland Rudkin registered it in 2003; the name honors his wife, who insisted he enter the seedling in a regional convention where it won best seedling. It went on to earn the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2012, the top honor for a Louisiana iris; grow it in full sun with steady moisture for best bloom.

common_name: Acadian Sky Louisiana Iris (Lavender-Blue Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fall in rich, moisture-retentive soil; Joseph Musacchia registered Acadian Sky in 2017 from a cross of 'Tchoupitoulas' x 'Queen Jeanne', and it won the AIS President's Cup in 2018 and the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2026.

directions: Acadian Sky is a tall, lavender-blue Louisiana iris with a green line signal outlined in deep purple, blooming midseason on sturdy stalks. Georgia hybridizer Joseph Musacchia registered it in 2017 from a cross of 'Tchoupitoulas' x 'Queen Jeanne', and it accumulated a strong award record including the AIS President's Cup in 2018 before taking the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2026. Site it in full sun in consistently moist to wet soil, where its height and clean color read well from a distance.

common_name: Rhonda Fleming Bearded Iris (White and Lilac Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Ron Mullin registered Rhonda Fleming in 1992, and it won the John C. Wister Medal in 1999.

directions: Rhonda Fleming is a ruffled, lightly laced tall bearded iris with white standards blending to lilac, darker lilac style arms, and white falls edged by a narrow solid lilac band. Ron Mullin registered it in 1992 from a cross of 'Go Around' x 'Laced Cotton' and named it for his lifelong favorite movie star; the cultivar won the John C. Wister Medal in 1999. Plant rhizomes shallow with tops exposed in well-drained, full-sun soil, and divide every three to four years.
sources: irises.org John C. Wister Medal records

common_name: Pond Lily Bearded Iris (Veronica Violet Reblooming Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Evelyn Jones registered Pond Lily in 1994, and it won the John C. Wister Medal in 2001.

directions: Pond Lily is a ruffled tall bearded iris in veronica violet, flushed deeper at the midrib with a hint of pink influence on the falls and tangerine beards, and it is capable of reblooming later in the season. Evelyn Jones registered it in 1994, and after earning an Honorable Mention and Award of Merit it went on to win the John C. Wister Medal in 2001. Grow it in full sun with sharp drainage, and keep spent bloom stalks removed to encourage a possible fall rebloom.
sources: irises.org John C. Wister Medal records

common_name: Local Color Bearded Iris (Roman Purple Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Keith Keppel registered Local Color in 1995, and it won the John C. Wister Medal in 2002.

directions: Local Color is a tall, imposing bearded iris with roman purple standards, slightly lighter style arms, and dark purple falls finished with a narrow violet edge and orange-vermilion beards; its foliage carries a purple-based tint. Keith Keppel registered it in 1995 from a cross of 'Witches' Sabbath' x 'Gallant Rogue', and after an Honorable Mention and Award of Merit it earned the John C. Wister Medal in 2002. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil, where its height and saturated color make a strong garden statement.
sources: irises.org John C. Wister Medal records

common_name: Spirit World Bearded Iris (Reddish Orchid Luminata Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Keith Keppel registered Spirit World in 1992, and it won the John C. Wister Medal in 2001.

directions: Spirit World is a fragrant tall bearded iris with medium reddish-orchid standards edged in smoky buff, and velvety red-purple falls showing slightly lighter luminata veining and reddish-orange beards set in an ivory circle. Keith Keppel registered it in 1992, and after an Honorable Mention and Award of Merit it won the John C. Wister Medal in 2001. It is noted as drought- and deer-resistant; grow it in full sun with well-drained soil for its best, most saturated color.
sources: irises.org John C. Wister Medal records

common_name: World Premier Bearded Iris (Blue-White and Blue-Violet Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Schreiner's Iris Gardens registered World Premier in 1998, and it won the John C. Wister Medal in 2004.

directions: World Premier is a ruffled tall bearded iris with blue-white standards and style arms and dark blue-violet falls rimmed in white, lit by yellow-based beards with a blue tint. Schreiner's Iris Gardens registered it in 1998 from a cross of 'Yaquina Blue' x an unknown seedling, and after Favorite Guest, Honorable Mention, and Award of Merit honors it earned the John C. Wister Medal in 2004. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil for its midseason-to-late bloom display.
sources: irises.org John C. Wister Medal records

common_name: Boogie Woogie Bearded Iris (White and Cloudy Violet Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Hooker Nichols registered Boogie Woogie in 1988 and introduced it in 1993, and it won the John C. Wister Medal in 1999.

directions: Boogie Woogie is a ruffled, laced tall bearded iris with white standards and cloudy violet falls marked with brown hafts, carried on sturdy mid-to-late-season stalks with orange-and-white beards. Louisiana hybridizer Hooker Nichols registered it in 1988 and introduced it in 1993; it collected the Fred and Barbara Walther Cup, Honorable Mention, and Award of Merit before winning the John C. Wister Medal in 1999. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil for best bloom and foliage health.
sources: irises.org John C. Wister Medal records

common_name: Marry The Night Bearded Iris (Dark Purple and White Banded Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Thomas Johnson registered Marry The Night in 2017, and it won the John C. Wister Medal in 2025.

directions: Marry The Night is an early-blooming, sweetly fragrant tall bearded iris with near-solid very dark purple standards and style arms set against pristine white falls precisely edged in dark purple, and orange beards tipped purple. Thomas Johnson registered it in 2017, and it won the John C. Wister Medal in 2025, one of three medals awarded that year alongside Keith Keppel's 'Dark Universe' and 'Ghirardelli Square'. Plant rhizomes shallow with tops exposed in full sun and well-drained soil for the strongest color contrast.
sources: World of Irises blog (theamericanirissociety.blogspot.com), 2025 Wister Medal announcement

common_name: Bright And Shining Star Bearded Iris (White Plicata Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil; Paul Black registered Bright And Shining Star in 2020.

directions: Bright And Shining Star is a spicy-fragrant, early-to-midseason tall bearded iris with white standards showing pale smoky violet style arms and brass-gold crests, and white falls finished with a narrow mid-purple stitched plicata band. Paul Black registered it in 2020, and it is actively grown and sold by multiple specialty iris nurseries. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil for crisp plicata patterning each spring.
